chunks.text: Darryl B. Daisey was born in 1961 into a Black and Nanticoke family in Lewes, Delaware. He is the identical twin brother of Darnell K. Daisey and one of eight children of William Harrison “Bill” Daisey Sr. and Shirley Corinne Street Daisey. The children, in the order given in their father’s obituary, are William Jr., Sarah, Deborah, Darnell, Darryl, Aida, Junina, and Dionne. [5] In August 1979 he and Darnell arrived at Penn State through the Black Scholars program. He majored in business logistics and graduated in May 1983 with a B.S. [6,14] He is the husband of Sari Daisey and the father of Benjamin and Warren Daisey. Warren asked for this biography. [52] Darryl compiled the Penn State University African American Chronicles and helped launch blackhistory.psu.edu. [22,24] The City of Lewes lists him as chairperson of the Lewes African American Heritage Commission, with a term running to Feb. 1, 2027. [70] On Dec. 6, 2025, the family’s new Lewes house was on the Holiday House Tour with a Black Santa theme. Darryl wrote that about 100 Black Santa figures and images and 100 Black Santa ornaments were displayed. [32,33] Since 2022 he has worked for Constellation. A company list dated August 2026 names him Principal Category Manager. His LinkedIn profile gives the title principal sourcing manager (Self-reported · LinkedIn). [51,20]

This book tells the life of Darryl B. Daisey in order, from the Lewes, Delaware, family he was born into in 1961 to the history commission he chairs today. It was written for his son Warren, who asked for a full biography instead of a list of accomplishments.

Every fact in it comes from a public source: newspapers such as The Daily Collegian, the Cape Gazette and the Delaware County Daily Times; Penn State’s La Vie yearbooks and the Penn State Black History website he helped build; City of Lewes and City of Dover records; Historic Lewes; Delaware Today; Delaware Public Media; university and award programs; and public company and university listings. Small gold numbers in the text point to the numbered source list, which is kept in a separate Word document, Darryl_Daisey_Sources.docx. That document gives the title, publisher, date and web address of each source and the pages of this book that use it. Some facts come only from what family members have posted about themselves on LinkedIn or in their own profiles. Those are marked (Self-reported · LinkedIn) or (Self-reported) . They have not been confirmed by an independent source.

Where sources disagree, the text says so. Where something could not be found, the text says that too. Nothing has been filled in by guesswork. The chapter on the family’s Black Santa collection, for example, uses only what the Cape Gazette and the family’s own public post report about it.

Every photograph is a real image from the credited source: a news photo, a family photo published with permission of the family, a yearbook page, a document, a screenshot of a source page, or a photo of a place. Where a source does not say who is in a photo or when it was taken, the caption says so. Where no photo of the person exists for an event, the book uses a photo of the place or the source document, and the caption says what it shows. No image was generated or altered to show a person. House numbers, a license plate and ticket numbers visible in a few photos were covered for privacy, and no personal email addresses or street addresses appear in this book.

How the book is organized. Part One traces the family roots in Lewes and the Nanticoke community, his parents, and a childhood that moved from Delaware to California, New Jersey and back. Part Two covers Penn State. Part Three follows his business career. Part Four is his work as Penn State’s Black history chronicler. Part Five returns to Lewes, where he became the family archivist and then chair of the city’s African American Heritage Commission. Part Six is about his family, and Part Seven about the things he collects and the legacy he is building.

Long before Darryl Daisey became a historian of other people’s stories, he was the product of one: a Black and Nanticoke family that has owned homes in Lewes, Delaware, since the nineteenth century. Lewes sits where Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, and it calls itself the First Town in the First State. For the Daisey family it is simply home. Over some 30 years of research with the help of relatives and friends, Darryl built a genealogy that reaches back to about 1773 and a man named Mills Coursey. Mills’ son John Coursey and John’s wife, Eliza Sammons, had a daughter, Lydia, who married James “Alfred” Daisey. [3]

Neither Lydia nor Alfred was ever taught to read or write. Even so, the couple bought a house in Lewes that the family still owns. Darnell Daisey later told the Cape Gazette that the house was purchased in 1880 and that many family members were born in it. “That house is most engrained in our family history,” he said. [3,4] Darryl’s great-grandmother, Sarah “Sallie” Waples Daisey, and her two siblings were born and raised there. Sarah had two children, one of whom was Darryl’s grandmother, Pearl Florine Daisey. In , formerly of Harbeson. [3,5] The family’s Native roots run through the Nanticoke, the Indian people of southern Delaware. Darryl’s father grew up near Indian Mission Church in the Lewes and Millsboro area, and his mother’s family, the Streets, came from Millsboro. His father would one day serve as chief of the Nanticoke Indian Tribe. [5]

One of Sarah’s brothers, William S. Daisey, served in World War I. The family believes he learned to drive in the Army. He also suffered lifelong complications from mustard gas, which led to his early death. A 1917 family photograph shows him in uniform with a service medal, and another from the 1920s shows him beside the Hotel Rodney Lewes and Rehoboth Auto Bus Line, which he operated. After the war he bought a house in Lewes and married Elsie Stockley. [3] Elsie outlived him by many decades. She remarried, moved out of the house and eventually sold it to her two godsons, Darryl and Darnell. She lived to 101 and died in 2000 as Elsie Daisey Draine. She left behind a gold-colored can full of old photographs. That can, which came to the twins and their siblings in April 2022, became the Daisey Family Legacy Photo Collection described in Part Five. [3,28]

The photos also brought back relatives Darryl barely remembered, such as Benjamin Harrison Daisey. He named his eldest son after him. The Cape Gazette called Benjamin Harrison Daisey his “great, great uncle” in the text of its 2023 story and his “great-uncle” in a photo caption. [3] Elsie’s legacy in numbers. By February 2023 the family had posted more than 350 of the photos on the “Memories of Lewes” Facebook page. Seventy were lent to the Lewes Historical Society, and the collection went on to supply many of the images in the 2024 Voices Heard exhibit. [3,29]

The Lewes in those photographs was a very different town from the one visitors see today. During the height of the menhaden fishing industry, according to a 2023 Cape Gazette report on the Lewes Historical Society’s Voices Heard documentaries, more than 40 percent of the town’s people were estimated to be African American. Today the estimate is 1 to 3 percent. Fish-factory owner and Lewes mayor Otis Smith provided jobs that paid enough to afford a mortgage, and he let the Black community use an open field that became its gathering place, with a baseball diamond and room for picnics. [39] Delaware Today gave similar figures in 2024: about 25 percent in the 1960s census, and about 1 percent now. [7]

Photographs from the Daisey Family Legacy Collection show that world. They include bands and majorettes marching in the Jolly Jills Social Club’s Memorial Day parade in the 1950s, when the parade ended at the open field where Shipcarpenter Square now stands, and the queen of the Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity’s Miss Sussex County pageant riding in a convertible. [40]

His parents were a self-made educator and politician who became a tribal chief, and a scout leader who opened doors for Black girls in Lewes. William Harrison “Bill” Daisey Sr. was born in Lewes on Oct. 20, 1931, during the Great Depression, and grew up near Indian Mission Church in the Lewes and Millsboro area. He started school at Lewes Elementary, the Hollyville School in Millsboro and the Richard Allen School in Georgetown. Because of segregation laws, however, the only way he could earn a high school diploma was to move 90 miles away, live with his grandmother and finish his senior year at Howard High School in Wilmington. [5] Delaware Today has noted that no Sussex County school awarded high school diplomas to Black or Native American students until 1950. [7]

He valued both an education and a trade. He became a qualified journeyman in more than eight trades and worked as an auto engine mechanic, body-shop foreman, aircraft painter, jet engine mechanic and engineering technician. While working full time, he earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Delaware State College and a master’s degree in administration from Glassboro State College, now Rowan University. [5] The Cape Gazette described him as one of 20 children. His obituary counted 12 surviving siblings and 17 who had died before him, so the sources do not agree on an exact number. [3,5] On March 25, 1951, he married Shirley Corinne Street, the daughter of Clarence Albert Street and Martha Ann Street of Millsboro. They were married for 63 years. [5]

Bill Daisey began his education career in adult education and training in New Jersey. While the family lived in Paulsboro he chaired the Paulsboro Recreation Committee and served on the Gloucester County Welfare Board. In 1978 he became vice principal of W.T. Chipman Middle School in Harrington, Delaware, and later transportation supervisor for the Lake Forest School District. He also spent five years as Kent County’s deputy recorder of deeds. He was president of the Dover Lions Club and of the Lower Delaware Principals Association, a Democratic committeeman, and vice chair of the Kent County Democrats. [5]

In 1987 he was elected to the Dover City Council, the first Native American and the second person of color elected to that post. He served three two-year terms. He sponsored a 1991 citywide ban on smoking in restaurants to help reduce cancer rates, ten years before the state passed its own, and he worked for fair employment opportunities for all Dover residents. [5] The council’s minutes from June 8, 1992, show “Mr. Daisey” moving and seconding the evening’s business, including a resolution honoring that year’s Miss Delaware Teen USA. [42]

His work with the Nanticoke Indian Tribe grew late in life. He was elected to the Tribal Council in 2004, chosen as assistant chief in 2008, and became chief in June 2013. As Chief William “Thunder Eagle” Daisey he served in what he called “the biggest honor of my life” until he stepped down for medical reasons in January 2016. He fondly remembered attending the 1963 March on Washington, where he sat 25 feet from Dr. King, as well as the 2008 inauguration of President Barack Obama and the opening of the National Museum of the American Indian. [5]

Shirley Daisey (1935–2014) was a Girl Scout leader for more than 30 years. [3] In the early 1960s the Lewes Girl Scout troop still did not admit African American or Native American girls. In 1963 a group of local mothers, with help from the existing troop, formed their own, and Shirley was one of its troop leaders. By the late 1960s the Lewes Girl Scouts were desegregated and the separate troop was disbanded. Shirley stayed active for more than 35 years and rose through the ranks of the Chesapeake Bay Girl Scout Council. [9]

Shirley came from a large Millsboro family. The 2009 obituary of her brother Albert Nelson Street Sr., a World War II medic, lists among his survivors a sister, “Shirley Daisey, of Delaware.” [44] She died on July 26, 2014. [5] When her children built a new family house in Lewes in 2025, they included “Shirley’s Pantry,” a tribute to the matriarch who loved to bake. [31]

Darryl and his twin, Darnell, were born in 1961 into a family that was already changing Lewes. Before they finished high school they had lived on both coasts.

The twins were two of William and Shirley’s eight children. Their father’s obituary lists the children in this order: William Jr., Sarah, Deborah, Darnell, Darryl, Aida, Junina and Dionne. [5] The family lived in Lewes, in a house their father bought, during the years when the town’s schools first opened to Black students. In September 1961 the formerly all-white Lewes public schools began admitting Black students on a voluntary basis. Six children of the Allen family and the three oldest Daisey children, William Jr., Sarah and Deborah, integrated the system. Sarah started first grade and Deborah kindergarten. [8,29,7] “Lewes was a small town; everyone knew everyone,” Darryl said in 2025, explaining how his family experienced it. “My father was more concerned with outsiders.” [30]

In 1965 the family left Lewes. Darryl has not lived there since, though his ties to the town never loosened. [3] The Daiseys moved to Oakland, California, where Darryl and Darnell went to Toler Heights Elementary School, a kindergarten-through-third-grade school that was mostly white with a small mix of Asian, Hispanic and Black students. His closest friends there were two white children, one Asian child and two Black children. He remembered only one early moment when race seemed to matter. At a carnival, an ice cream vendor kept serving white customers ahead of the twins, until their mother marched them away, saying “we would get our ice cream somewhere else!” [11]

On April 4, 1968, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis. In April 1985, two years after graduating from Penn State, Darryl wrote a forum essay for The Daily Collegian about the day Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated. He was almost seven years old and in first grade in Oakland. Near the end of the school day, he wrote, a crowd of about 50 young people gathered outside shouting “they shot him,” and bricks came through the classroom windows. The students were herded into the auditorium, where the principal announced that Dr. King had been shot in Memphis. [11]

His mother walked the twins home past broken windows and smoke from distant fires. His sisters Sarah, 12, and Debbie, 10, were already home. His oldest brother, Billy, 16, came in later. Billy had been caught up in the violence at his high school, and he and some friends had escorted white teenagers from the neighborhood home safely, which made him something of a local hero. When the evening news reported that Dr. King had died, the house went quiet. “My mom was the first to start crying,” Darryl wrote. His parents had been active in the civil rights movement, and his father had taken part in the 1963 March on Washington. [11]

The essay ends with a line that sums up much of what came later in his life: “Over the years, the teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. have played a big part in shaping my values, beliefs and the way I deal with people who are different from me… The ironic part was that I started to get to know who Dr. King was on the day he died.” [11] “A lot of people say young adults my age are too young to remember. I remember. I just thank God I was too young to hate because of it.”Darryl B. Daisey, The Daily Collegian, April 10, 1985 The Daiseys left Oakland in April 1969, and, as the twins wrote in 1985, neither of them ever went back. [11] The family settled in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in Gloucester County. Their father chaired the town’s recreation committee and served on the Gloucester County Welfare Board while he worked in adult education and training. [5,10]

In 1978 the family moved back to Delaware, this time to Dover, when Bill Daisey became a vice principal in Harrington. [5] The move came about a year before the twins finished high school. Alumni directories list both Darryl and Darnell with Dover High School’s Class of 1979. Darryl also appears in a Paulsboro High School Class of 1979 listing, which fits a family that moved between the two towns. Darryl’s Dover High profile on that site was created by its member, so this book treats it as self-reported. [13] When the twins reached Penn State, La Vie listed their hometown as Dover, Delaware. [12] Looking back. In his 1985 essay Darryl thanked his parents “for not letting the memory of him [Dr. King] to exit from my life.” In August 1979 he left Dover for Penn State, where, as he later put it, he joined organizations because “I like to change things and make things happen.” [2] [11]

chunks.chapter: “A Big School With a Big Name”
chunks.text: In late August 1979 the Daisey twins arrived at University Park as part of Penn State’s Black Scholars program. Neither had seen the campus before. “I had applied to one school to go to college: Penn State,” Darryl said in his recorded interview for the African American Chronicles. “I never saw Penn State. I actually got a partial scholarship. It was called the Black Scholars Program.” [14] In 2018 he told The Daily Collegian that he chose the university because it was “a big school with a big name.” He majored in business logistics, the field now called supply chain management. [2]

chunks.chapter: “A Big School With a Big Name”
chunks.text: The twins roomed together for their first couple of years. “Being identical twins kind of attracted attention,” he recalled, “so we really had… a lot of friends quickly. We got involved with a lot of things very quickly.” [14] Penn State was overwhelmingly white. In four years he had one African American faculty member, in a Black studies class, and so the brothers became “involved with recruiting… to attract more students and faculty members.” He also worked as a campus tour guide. [14,48] Some details of daily life stuck with him. He wore an Afro most of the time, he said, because there were “no places in State College that cut or styled African-American’s hair.” He had to wait until he went home to get a haircut. [2] It was also an eventful era: the football team won its first national championship in 1982, and Bryce Jordan succeeded John Oswald as president in 1983. [2]

chunks.chapter: “A Big School With a Big Name”
chunks.text: One photograph from those years has become a family favorite. It shows Darryl and Darnell with head football coach Joe Paterno in 1982, the year Penn State won its first national championship. Darryl stands on the right in a red T-shirt that says “Dover, Del.” Paterno was also one of the speakers at the first Brotherhood Day, which Darnell chaired in 1981 . [2,15]

chunks.chapter: “A Big School With a Big Name”
chunks.text: “I like to change things and make things happen and those organizations allowed me to do that.”Darryl Daisey on USG, the Black Student Union and his work as an RA, The Daily Collegian, 2018 He kept the friendships. In 2018 he said he had made lifelong friends at Penn State and that “the Penn State connection” helped him make business contacts. He was visiting campus about once a year and noted how much it had changed: it was bigger and “clearly more diverse,” with more African American, Hispanic and international students. [2]

By his senior year Darryl had become a familiar name in Penn State’s student government. He used the job to remove small barriers that most students never noticed.The La Vie 1983 yearbook lists him as “Darryl B. Daisey, Dover DE, B Log, USG—Senator—Sup Crt, Blk Std Union, RA, WEHR.” That made him a business logistics major, an Undergraduate Student Government senator and a member of its Supreme Court, a Black Student Union member, a Resident Assistant, and a member of WEHR. Darnell is listed just above him: “B Log, USG, Blk Std Union, RA.” Both twins appear in the USG group photos in the 1982 and 1983 yearbooks. [12]

What the yearbook tells us. In 1982 and 1983 the twins were active in USG, where Darryl served in both the Senate and the student Supreme Court, and in the East Halls Residence Association, the Black Student Union and Delta Nu Alpha. Both also worked as Resident Assistants. [12]

On Feb. 11, 1982, according to Penn State’s Black History timeline, an East Halls Black Student Union representative “uncovers that Penn State’s long time ‘mandatory’ swim test/class was never really mandatory. When Darryl Daisey questioned the ‘policy’, he discovered it was never really a requirement at all,” even though it had been presented that way for more than 48 years. The change “removed a small barrier to minority recruitment.” [16] That September the Collegian reported that Daisey, a USG senator, had met with the physical education program’s advisory committee. “I think it should be optional all the time,” he said. [49] On April 1, 1982, four African American students won seats in the 35-member USG Senate: Keith Burris from East Halls, Charles Blackwell from Nittany Halls, and “twins Darnell and Darryl Daisey,” who were re-elected from East Halls. [17]

That fall Darryl chaired the USG Senate Transportation Advisory Committee. On Dec. 10, 1982, the Collegian reported that, under an agreement between the Senate and the Office of the Vice President for Business, the Campus Loop bus would run until 2:30 a.m. on Friday and Saturday nights on a trial basis, with free rides after 11 p.m. If the Loop did not lose money, Daisey said, the new hours would become permanent. [18]

He had data to back the idea: an earlier spring trial had raised weekend ridership by about 300. But his main concern was safety, especially for women walking home alone late at night and students tempted to drive drunk or ride with a drunk driver. “People complain that if they go to fraternity parties, there is no safe way to get home,” he said. “This is a nice situation — everyone gains. I expect the loop to gain a marginal income, and this is a chance to give the students a service.” [18] “There is no question that the loop will make money this weekend. In the long run, since Penn State has such bad weather, they’ll make money.”Darryl Daisey, The Daily Collegian, Dec. 10, 1982

Outside student government, the twins helped start a campus tradition and joined the professional society of their major.Brotherhood Day was first held on May 6, 1981, to “enhance awareness of the positive results of unity and the negative effects of racism and separatism.” It was conceived by the East Halls Black Student Union and the East Halls Residence Association, and it was chaired by Darnell Daisey. Over the next three years it brought Julian Bond, Benjamin Hooks and Martin Luther King III to campus. [15] Darryl remembered it as “the day to try to unite the races,” with speakers including “Julian Bond, Benjamin Hooks, Martin Luther King III, [and] Joe Paterno.” [14]

Both twins also appear in the 1983 La Vie photo of Delta Nu Alpha, the professional transportation and logistics fraternity. Its main goal, the yearbook says, was “to bring in speakers from business corporations relating to the business logistics field.” [12] In May 1983 Darryl graduated with a B.S. in business logistics. A photo from that day shows him with his friends Racine Leonard (Davis) and Anya Armstrong (Edwards) and with Darnell, who earned the same degree. [47,11] The university did not forget him. In 1987 the Department of Business Logistics gave him an outstanding service award. He later became a Life Member of the Penn State Alumni Association and a member of its Golden Lion Society. [6]

For more than four decades Darryl has worked in the field he studied at Penn State: buying, moving and managing what large companies need, and making room for minority-owned suppliers. By the spring of 1985 Darryl was a distribution analyst at the Dow Chemical Company in Midland, Michigan. Darnell was in management at Bell of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and their parents were living in Dover. [11] His LinkedIn profile also lists positions with IBM, PricewaterhouseCoopers, Dade Behring and DuPont (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [20] The 2019 Chicago awards program confirms the Dade Behring years: it says that while at Dade Behring (printed “Dade Bearing”) and later at American Water, he “created the business case, formalized and managed supplier diversity programs for two organizations.” [26]

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Darryl was in Arlington, Virginia, for a business meeting, not far from the Pentagon, which was struck by a hijacked airliner. That same morning his twin was in a building next to the World Trade Center . [19] From 2003 to 2014 he worked at American Water, the utility company, in supply chain roles that his LinkedIn profile says included senior supplier relationship and project sourcing manager and interim chief supply officer (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [20] The Delaware County Daily Times confirmed in 2014 that he worked there, when his sons gave a health presentation to American Water employees . [21] 2022–present: Constellation; listed as Principal Category Manager in 2026 [51,20]

In 2015 he joined Exelon in Philadelphia, the parent company of utilities including PECO, ComEd, Delmarva Power and Baltimore Gas and Electric, as a principal category manager. [26] In 2018 The Daily Collegian identified him as “a principle sourcing manager at Exelon from Garnet Valley, Pennsylvania.” [2] At Exelon he managed the enterprise-wide supplemental labor category, including the Management Services Program for staff-augmentation workers. Over three years he helped lead a program that produced “a significant increase in Tier II diverse spending,” meaning more of the program’s spending reached diverse subcontractors, such as minority-owned businesses. [26]

That work earned him a public honor. At the 52nd Chicago Business Opportunity Fair, held April 17–18, 2019, the Chicago Minority Supplier Development Council’s Minority Business Enterprise Input Committee named Darryl Daisey of Exelon one of its Outstanding Buyers of the Year. The other honorees came from the University of Chicago and Chicago Public Schools. [26] His LinkedIn profile lists the same award as “Outstanding Buyer 2019.” [20] Since 2022 he has worked for Constellation, the energy company. His LinkedIn profile gives his title as principal sourcing manager (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [20] Constellation’s own supplier contact list, dated August 2026, names him Principal Category Manager for categories including business consulting, customer service, financial services and mass markets. [51]

In November 2007, after registering for the 2008 Black Alumni Reunion, Darryl “was somewhat surprised to discover there was no documented comprehensive account of the African American experience at Penn State.” He decided to write one. He set out, he wrote, to compile “a brief historical timeline.” With help from Penn State staff, alumni, family and friends, it grew into the Penn State University African American Chronicles. [24] He did it from a distance. In February 2008 the Collegian reported that “Daisey began work on the timeline in November, but he hasn’t set foot on campus for two years. He’s doing his research online and through the help of different offices at Penn State.” Penn State kept no records by race before 1970, so he relied on Black alumni and on old newspapers and yearbooks. [22]

On April 18, 2008, the roughly 50-page Chronicles, 1899–2008 was given to everyone at the Black Alumni Reunion. Many considered it “the first comprehensive account of the African American experience at Penn State.” [23,22] In the acknowledgments he thanked his wife, Sari, who proofread it, and “two young sons, Benjamin and Warren, for putting up with the late nights, phone calls, and time away from the family as I researched this document.” [52]

“The attendees were the only people who had it, and I wanted students, faculty and alumni to have access to the information as well,” he told the Collegian in January 2009, after launching an informal site and then PennStateBlackHistory.com. [53] On Sept. 10, 2010, the official site, blackhistory.psu.edu, launched at the 2010 Black Alumni Reunion. Penn State Public Broadcasting (WPSU) built it with sponsorship from the Office of Educational Equity, based on his revised Chronicles. It has a chronology, photos, video interviews, historical documents and news footage, and its copyright line reads “© Darryl B. Daisey and WPSU Penn State.” [24,25]

Student leaders used it right away. Christian Ragland, the first Black president of the University Park Undergraduate Association, said: “I can always reflect back on those who came before me — to know that as an African American, I didn’t do it alone.” NAACP chapter president Travis Salters said he used the site in his organization’s meetings. [25] Penn State University Libraries now holds three editions of the Chronicles: 1899–2008, 1899–2010 and 1899–2016 (call number LD4481.P82 D35). [54] More history projects. In August 2010 he compiled Penn State African American Firsts, a 14-page list of firsts in enrollment, athletics, leadership and the arts. [55] The Africana Research Center’s Pioneering African American Faculty & Staff (revised February 2011) thanks “Darryl Daisey for the unconditional support and major resources.” [56]

The Collegian’s 2017 coverage called him “founder of The Penn State Black History Project,” which he carries on with the Office of Educational Equity, the Africana Research Center, the African and African American Studies Department, the Penn State Alumni Association and the Paul Robeson Cultural Center. [27,6] In February 2019, for a Black History Month story, the Collegian traced the path of Black history at Penn State through his work. [47] In October 2024 the paper interviewed “Darryl Daisey, researcher and compiler of Penn State African American Chronicles” about Calvin H. Waller, Penn State’s first Black graduate, in 1905. “Waller certainly started the tradition of excellence,” Daisey said. [57] That same fall, The Penn Stater alumni magazine devoted its editor’s column to him (see the Epilogue). [1]

“History tells you why you’re here. It makes me feel blessed and appreciative of what people did before me, but also motivates me to want to continue to move things forward.”Darryl Daisey, The Daily Collegian, April 3, 2025 [48]

He has returned to campus again and again to teach students the history he documented: the triumphs, and also what he calls “the good, the bad, and the ugly.”Penn State All-Sports Museum, Feb. 23, 2011 The All-Sports Museum chose Daisey, “the founder of www.blackhistory.psu.edu,” as a speaker in its 2011 Black History Month series alongside ESPN’s Lisa Salters (’88). He spoke at noon in the museum’s Clemens Family Theatre. [59] “Although I do plan to talk about past Penn State’s African American athletes, my focus is to also broaden the discussion to more than just sports,” he said. “I want to talk about the ‘lost legends’ in other areas too.” [60]

The Penn State chapter of the NAACP hosted “accomplished business professional and amateur historian Darryl Daisey” for “Penn State African American History… Shaping a Stronger Community Today” in the HUB Flex Theatre. [61] He spoke about Mildred Settle Bunton, the first African American woman to attend and graduate from Penn State; Cumberland Posey; the Douglass Association; and Lincoln Hall. He did not shy away from “darker instances in Penn State’s past.” And he urged students to learn from older leaders while they can: “We missed out on some really valuable folks we could have learned from.” [27] That month the chapter gave him its Carter G. Woodson Award (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [20]

Back in LewesHis talks are not limited to State College. On Feb. 16, 2023, he presented the Daisey Family History to the Lewes African American Heritage Commission. On Feb. 13, 2025, he gave the Historic Lewes Speaker Series talk “A New View, The Daisey Family Legacy Photo Collection” at the Lewes History Museum, and that same month he moderated a panel on the integration of the Lewes schools (Part Five). [3,28,30]

The Paul Robeson Cultural Center and the Department of African American Studies invited him back for a lunch-and-learn in the Flex Theater of the HUB-Robeson Center. [63] The Collegian called him “Curator of the Penn State Black History, African American Chronicles.” He spoke about Guion Bluford, Keegan-Michael Key, Julie Cromitie, Dave and Harry Alston, H. Jesse Arnelle and Lincoln Hall. Student Dinaye Smith said: “He had a passion by the way he was speaking about these figures.” His nephew Bryce, a Penn State finance student, was in the audience. [48]

He supports Penn State with his money as well as his research, especially the scholarships and programs that help Black students.Wally Triplett and a scholarship auction, 2012 Wally Triplett was a Penn State football pioneer who went on to the NFL. In 2012 he came to the Penn State Black Alumni Reunion to be honored. “My wife and I were assigned to pick up Wally Triplett and his wife at the Lewistown Train Station and bring them to the 2012 Penn State Black Alumni Reunion, where he was to be honored,” Daisey told Onward State. Warned in advance that Triplett “did not sign plastic helmets because he never played in them,” Daisey found two mini leather helmets, which Triplett signed. “I kept one helmet, and donated the other to be auctioned to help fund a scholarship.” [65]

chunks.chapter: The Photographs in the Gold Can
chunks.text: After his father died, Darryl found himself the keeper of more than a century of Lewes history, stored in a can left behind by his godmother. William Daisey Sr. died on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 25, 2021. Shortly afterward his children began going through the family photographs and filling in their history. [3,5] In April 2022, less than a year after their father’s death, Darryl and his siblings came into possession of the cache of photos that their great-great-aunt Elsie Daisey Draine had kept in an old gold-colored can. [28]

chunks.chapter: The Photographs in the Gold Can
chunks.text: In September 2022 the family came across the “Memories of Lewes” Facebook page, and Darryl began posting the pictures there. By February 2023 they had shared more than 350, and community members helped identify the people and events in them. “Unbeknownst to him and his family,” Historic Lewes later wrote, “the photos offered a rare glimpse into the African American history of Lewes from the late 1800s through the 1960s.” [3,28] Trina Brown-Hicks, an administrator of the page and a member of the heritage commission, said: “I thought that history was lost there. I thought we could not find pictures from the ’20s or the ’30s, let alone the 1800s.” [3]

chunks.chapter: The Photographs in the Gold Can
chunks.text: On Feb. 16, 2023, Darryl presented the Daisey Family History to the Lewes African American Heritage Commission. J. Marcos Salaverria, director of education at the Lewes Historical Society, called the photographs “essentially what you call a historian’s dream.” The family lent the society 70 of them. “We hope it will not only help, but enrich the telling of the African American story of Lewes,” Darryl said. “My grandmother and my great-grandmother would be thrilled to know that they were helpful in telling that story.” [3]

chunks.chapter: The Photographs in the Gold Can
chunks.text: The collection is now cited as the “Daisey Family Legacy Collection” in local reporting. It has supplied images for the Cape Gazette’s stories on the Jolly Jills parade and on the Black Girl Scout troops of the 1960s, and for the 2024 Voices Heard exhibit. [40,9,29] One of the oldest photographs, of Mary P. (Miller) Wolfe, who was born in Lewes in the 1820s, is believed to be one of the oldest known images of Lewes. [7]

The family photographs helped complete a documentary and a record-setting museum exhibit about Black life in Lewes. According to Historic Lewes, the Daisey photos “would be used to facilitate and enrich the completion of the ‘Voices Heard: The History and Legacy of the Black Community in Lewes’ documentary and exhibit.” [28] The Lewes Historical Society’s second documentary, Voices Heard: African American Life and Legacy in Lewes Part II, was produced with 302 Stories Inc. and screened in the summer of 2023. At that screening Darnell walked his sons through a family album in the theater lobby. [39]

The exhibit opened at the Lewes History Museum with a reception on April 19, 2024. Darryl, whose family is prominently featured, said more than 100 people came. Delaware Today counted 150 visitors, including members of the late Langston Hughes’ family, and the historical society said attendance set a record for one of its exhibits. [29,7] The exhibit featured about 30 photographs (Delaware Today said 28) from the late 1800s to the 1960s, many shown publicly for the first time and many on loan from the Daisey Family Legacy Collection. Visitors were greeted by a late-1800s charcoal sketch of James “Alfred” Daisey and his grandson, William S. Daisey. [29,7]

“Our ancestors would be very proud that they are part of the story of African Americans in Lewes,” Darryl said. “It is a positive portrayal of our history.” And on the response to his online posts: “I didn’t expect such an overwhelming response. People recognized their family members and started sharing stories about the pictures.” [29,7] “Only the tip of the iceberg.” Trina Brown-Hicks, who led the push for the documentary and exhibit, told reporters it was “only the tip of the iceberg in terms of sharing the journey of the Black community of Lewes.” Salaverria called the exhibit “the end of a three-year project, but… just the beginning of the research to complete the narrative.” [29]

A Lewes city panel created in 2020 to preserve local Black history became Darryl’s second civic home. By 2026 he was its chair. The Mayor and City Council established the Lewes African American Heritage Commission on Jan. 13, 2020, “to preserve the historical contributions and educate the public regarding the history and contributions made by the African American Community in Lewes, DE.” [70] In 2023 the Rev. George Edwards was its chair. [39] The City of Lewes now lists Darryl Daisey as Chairperson, with a term running to Feb. 1, 2027, and 2026 news stories identify him as chair. [70,34,36]

Among the commission’s documents is the Lewes Delaware Black History Timeline, “Compiled by Darryl B. Daisey for the Lewes African American Heritage Commission.” It is a 10-page history running from 1631 to the present and was last updated in June 2026. [8] In July 2025, WMDT 47abc’s “Brightside” segment profiled the commission’s work, including the renaming of the formerly segregated beach as Johnnie Walker Beach. [71]

For the commission’s 2025 Black History Month program at Lewes Elementary School, he moderated a panel of five of the nine Allen and Daisey family members who desegregated the Lewes public schools in 1961 and 1962. Two of the panelists were his sisters, Sarah (Daisey) Minor and Deborah (Daisey) Street. He “laid out the timeline that led up to the integration of Lewes schools,” from Delaware’s 1875 Jim Crow law to Brown v. Board of Education. The city gave the panelists proclamations, and the commission gave them certificates of appreciation. [30]

A year later the commission hosted a gathering of people who grew up on the Lewes Community Playground, a field in the middle of the town’s African American neighborhood where children played from 1957 until the land was sold in 1978. It is now the Shipcarpenter Square development. Darryl, as commission chair, served as emcee. Panelists remembered May Day celebrations, Jolly Jills events, Sunday “van shows,” and baseball games where Black and white children began playing together years before the schools integrated. Mayor Amy Marasco announced a working group on historical markers that could recognize the site. [34]

During segregation, Lewes Beach 2 was the city’s beach for Black residents and visitors. Johnnie Walker, an entrepreneur, ran a restaurant and dance hall there from 1958 to the early 1970s and helped make it “a place of community, joy and pride.” The beach now bears his name, and an interpretive sign with the only known photo of Walker was installed in June 2026. [36,35]

A replica of the beach’s old wooden pavilion has been a priority for the commission. In August 2026 Delaware Public Media reported that Daisey, as chair, “voiced some concerns” that site plans had been held up with the city’s engineering firm for months, delaying a long approval process. “I thought we could do it by 2027, but everything you’re telling me says no,” he told the city’s parks administrator. “But if it stays in GMB, then the summer of 2028 is in jeopardy.” [35] A month later, on Sept. 19, the commission hosted its fifth annual Johnnie Walker Beach Day, where many attendees wore shirts reading “Ancestral Sands.” [36]

The Girl Scout story his mother helped write came full circle in 2026. In 2025 the commission began gathering information and photos about the Black troop formed in Lewes in 1963, hoping to organize a reunion. [9] On Oct. 14, 2026, it and the Girl Scouts of the Chesapeake Bay hosted “Bridging the Promise: Girl Scouts Then & Now” at Bethel United Methodist Church, where both the Black and white troops once met. [73,37] The Cape Gazette reported that Darryl Daisey organized the event. Five former members of the Black troop, including his sisters Sarah Daisey Minor and Deborah Daisey Street, answered questions from young scouts from Lewes, Milton and Rehoboth Beach, who played reporters for the evening. Each scout received a patch reading “A Journey to the Past.” [37]

“We shared the same values found in the [Girl Scout] promise: courage, confidence, character and service. All of the ladies who were part of that segregated troop have kept that promise in some way.”Janet Maull-Martin, former member of the Black troop, Oct. 14, 2026 [37]

Their father wanted his children to keep the family’s Lewes properties so the next generation would stay connected to the town. Keeping that promise took years. In 2020 the siblings began talking with their father about what to do with the three Lewes properties he owned: the house he had bought in Lewes, the house William S. Daisey had bought after World War I, and the family homestead purchased in 1880. William Daisey was adamant that they keep them, so that the next generation would stay connected to Lewes. He died in 2021, before the fight began. [31,3,4]

The siblings started with the largest lot. Because the house was in the city’s historic district, they had to apply to the Historic Preservation Architectural Review Commission, which they did in 2022. “We thought that we should be able to get this easily approved. Boy, were we wrong,” Darnell said. “We realized that we have stepped into a much bigger issue in Lewes… the fact that a once-thriving African American community in Lewes had been decimated.” After an often-contentious process, the commission approved demolition in August 2023, and the old house came down in March 2024. [31]

On May 7, 2025, the family opened the new four-bedroom house, designed by local builder James Burgess, to thank the community. “This is a celebration to show our appreciation to everyone who helped us achieve our parents’ goals and wishes here in Lewes,” Darnell said. Darryl said he, his brother and their five sisters all had input into the plans. “We weren’t looking to build a mansion. We wanted to build someplace that could be lasting.” Incoming Mayor Amy Marasco praised the family’s graciousness. [31]

The second property, the house William S. Daisey had bought after World War I and that Elsie later sold to her godsons, was under renovation in 2025 when a building inspector found termites. The city condemned it, and the 155-year-old house was demolished in August 2025. On Nov. 6, 2025, the review commission voted 5–0 to approve the twins’ plans for a new house on the site, after the family agreed to several design changes and won a variance to move it two feet back from the sidewalk and two feet from the neighboring property. “We feel relieved that we can now complete the building of the house that we’ve been trying to build for two-plus years,” Darnell said. “We’re happy that future generations will keep using that house and stay engaged in the City of Lewes,” Darryl said. [4]

The 1880 homestead is next. “That house is most engrained in our family history,” Darnell said. “It was purchased in 1880, and [many family members] were born in that house.” [4] “This is a big investment for us. They are very meaningful to our family, something that will last for generations to come.”Darryl Daisey, Cape Gazette, May 12, 2025 [31]

Darnell K. Daisey went through every stage of Darryl’s early life with him: Lewes, Oakland, Paulsboro, Dover High School’s Class of 1979, and Penn State. [11,13] He also earned a business logistics degree in 1983. La Vie lists him in USG, the Black Student Union and as a Resident Assistant, and he was re-elected to the USG Senate alongside Darryl in 1982. [12,17] He chaired Penn State’s first Brotherhood Day in 1981. [15] By 1985 he was working in management for Bell of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. [11]

On Sept. 11, 2001, Darnell and two coworkers flew from Boston to New York to give a business presentation in a building next to the World Trade Center. “We entered the West Street building at approximately 8:45 a.m. and took the elevator up to the fifth floor. We had just begun heading to the conference room when all of a sudden the building shook,” he later wrote in a memoir he titled “Too Close to Realize.” The men saw people falling from the towers and the buildings collapse, then walked 55 blocks uptown over three and a half hours. They spent the night at the New York Yacht Club, and the next day he took Amtrak home to Maryland. Darryl, meanwhile, was at a meeting in Arlington, Virginia, not far from the Pentagon. [19]

Twenty-five years later Darnell reflected: “My overwhelming feeling is a deep appreciation for life… Ultimately, experiencing that day taught me to deeply appreciate the special people in my life and treasure every single moment we have together.” [19] Darnell and his wife, Lisa, were donors to the 2008 Black Alumni Reunion scholarship, and he is thanked in the Chronicles. [67,52] He and Darryl are the godsons of Elsie Daisey Draine, who sold them a family house. [3] In Lewes he became the family’s main spokesman during the long fight over the houses, and in 2023 he walked his sons through the family album at the Voices Heard screening. [31,4,39]

Darryl’s five sisters and older brother appear in the public record as trailblazers, scouts and keepers of family history. William H. Daisey Jr., called Billy, was the oldest. In Oakland on the day Dr. King was killed, the 16-year-old and a couple of friends escorted white teenagers from their neighborhood home safely through the riots. “In the days to follow, he became somewhat of a hero in the neighborhood,” Darryl wrote. Earlier, in Lewes, he was one of the three oldest Daisey children who integrated the town’s schools. [11,8]

Sarah L. (Daisey) Minor entered first grade and Deborah A. (Daisey) Street kindergarten when they integrated the Lewes schools in 1962. [29,30] “Anyone who thought maybe Black kids were not as smart as white kids, we dispelled that myth,” Sarah said in 2025. “We were able to open the door for other people, and I’m proud of that.” Deborah’s message for children today was “You can make a difference.” [30] Sarah was in the 1963 Brownie troop, and both sisters helped the heritage commission reconstruct the history of the Black Girl Scout troop their mother led. In October 2026 they shared those memories with a new generation of scouts. [9,37] The obituary of their father also names Aida “Mam” Binateeq, who lives in Saudi Arabia; Junina N. Sullivan; and Dionne L. Williford, who appears with her siblings at the 2025 house celebration. [5,31]

Eight children, a wide family. At their father’s death in 2021 the eight Daisey children had given William and Shirley 18 grandchildren and 21 great-grandchildren. [5] Darryl has said that he, his brother and their five sisters all had input into the new Lewes house. [31]

Darryl and his wife, Sari, raised their two sons in Garnet Valley, Pennsylvania. Each has built a public record of his own. Sari (Rosemond) Daisey proofread the first Chronicles, and Darryl thanked her and their “two young sons, Benjamin and Warren,” for putting up with the late nights it took. [5,52] She was among the donors to the 2008 reunion scholarship. [67] She holds a master’s degree, and in 2024 and 2025 she wrote publicly about “Parenting with Pride,” including an article on Medium, and spoke with Warren on a panel of that name at a workplace event (Self-reported) . [74,75,76]

In July 2014 the Delaware County Daily Times reported that Benjamin, then a Garnet Valley Middle School student, had made a health-class presentation on the effects of diet soda. It persuaded his father to give up soda, and American Water invited Benjamin to speak at three of the company’s Healthy Start Challenge Rallies in Voorhees and Cherry Hill, N.J. Warren, then eight and about to start third grade, helped present. “Both Benjamin and Warren did a wonderful job,” said wellness manager Margaret Fenner-Gulledge. [21] “Getting this public speaking opportunity will serve them both well in the future… Doing well here helps to build their confidence in their ability to not only speak in public, but also in selling their ideas.”Sari and Darryl Daisey, Delaware County Daily Times, 2014 [21]

Darryl named his eldest son for Benjamin Harrison Daisey, the relative who appears in the family photographs. [3] Benjamin Daisey studied music technology at Temple University’s Boyer College of Music and Dance. Temple’s Spring 2024 capstone program lists his project, Clockwork (A LiaChorus EP): the recording, editing and mixing of a four-song EP by LiaChorus, a Temple a cappella group of 16 singers and a vocal percussionist, in which he also sang. The program describes him as “an experienced audio engineer who specializes in vocal work, and live sound” and says he would graduate in 2024 with a Bachelor of Science in Music Technology. [77] Temple choral programs from 2020 to 2022 list a Benjamin Daisey singing with the University Singers, and his LinkedIn profile lists the 2024 degree (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [78,79]

Warren Daisey, the younger son, is a student at Commonwealth University of Pennsylvania’s Bloomsburg campus. The university’s Senate membership list names him as an undergraduate representative (Bloomsburg) on its Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging Committee. [80] His own LinkedIn posts describe a run of competition results (Self-reported · LinkedIn) : he competed in the Keystone Sales Challenge sponsored by Sherwin-Williams, his first sales competition. In October 2026 he reached the semifinals of the Commonwealth University Sales Contest sponsored by Cintas, and on Oct. 15, 2026, he won first place and $500 at Susquehanna University’s 3rd Annual Quick Pitch Sales Challenge. He also reports winning a year-long award for informative speaking in speech and debate. [81,82,83,84]

He has spoken publicly alongside his mother. Their “Parenting with Pride” panel, he wrote, was a meaningful experience for both of them (Self-reported · LinkedIn) . [76] Twelve years after helping his brother present to American Water employees, the eight-year-old co-presenter had become a prize-winning speaker. [21,83]A note on sources. Warren’s committee seat comes from a public Commonwealth University listing. His competition results come from his own public LinkedIn posts and are marked self-reported. The 2014 presentation comes from the Delaware County Daily Times. [80,21]

chunks.text: The family history work has already reached the next generation.Darnell’s sons, Bryce and Cameron, have joined the family history work. At the 2023 screening of Voices Heard, the brothers looked through a family album in the theater lobby while their father identified the people in it. [39] Bryce Daisey became a Penn State finance student. As a second-year student in 2025 he told the Collegian that he “grew up going to Penn State football games” and got an early look at his uncle’s project. He is listed as the primary contact for the 6:17 Men’s Fellowship student organization at University Park. [48,85] His advice to other students: “If you have a dream and if you have an ambition, act on it… There’s a ton of Black excellence and Black achievements coming from this PWI that a lot of people don’t know about.” [48]

chunks.text: Photograph: Black Santa nutcrackers flank the fireplace beneath two stockings stitched “Daisey,” in a photo from the family’s Holiday House Tour post. Photo posted by Darryl Daisey · Facebook group “African American Christmas Decorators & MORE....”, Dec. 7, 2025.

On Dec. 6, 2025, the Daisey family opened their new Lewes house to the public with a theme that was theirs alone: Black Santa. Every December, Historic Lewes, the Lewes Historical Society, raises money for its preservation and education work with the Holiday House Tour of Lewes. In 2025 the self-guided tour took place on Saturday, Dec. 6, from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. It featured ten private homes and two public buildings, among them the Daughters of the American Revolution’s Thomas Maull House and the lobby of The Lodge at Historic Lewes, plus a Holiday Village and Market on the society’s campus. A $50 ticket came with a guidebook describing each property, which also served as admission, and volunteer docents from local nonprofits were on hand to share each home’s story. [86,87,32]

One of the ten homes was the new Daisey family house, the house the family had fought for years to build and had opened to the community seven months earlier . [32,31] The Cape Gazette’s photo coverage shows Darryl in the living room, beside a tree hung with Santa ornaments, “tell[ing] the story and history of the Daisey family” to a crowd of visitors. Framed photographs from the family collection stood on easels through the house. The paper reported that “an extensive collection of African American Santas is among the historical photographs from the Daisey family,” and that “the Daisey family’s exhibition is available to view among the extensive collection of African American Santas.” [32]

The night after the tour, Darryl posted an album about it in a Facebook group called “African American Christmas Decorators & MORE....” The page lists him as the author. The post reads in full: [33] “Family participated in the annual Holiday House Tour in Lewes, Delaware yesterday and our theme was Black Santa. About 100 of our Black Santa figures/images and 100 Black Santa ornaments were displayed, with the tree being a big hit.”Darryl Daisey, Facebook, Dec. 7, 2025 [33]

The album shows how the collection filled the house. Black Santa nutcrackers flank the fireplace under stockings stitched with the family name. The tree is hung with Santa ornaments and ringed with Santa figures. More figures crowd the living-room table. A Black Santa painting watches over the dining table, and a framed Black Santa portrait and a Santa bedspread decorate a bedroom. In the kitchen, a Black Santa and Mrs. Claus stand on the counter beside the cookie jars. [33] By the time this book was prepared, the post had drawn 191 reactions. “Beautiful. Love the Santas by the fireplace,” one group member wrote. Another wrote, “This is all so well done!! Im sure it was a hit!!” [33]

The tour brought together the two collections that define Darryl’s Lewes years. The Black Santas were displayed alongside the family photographs that Elsie Daisey Draine saved in her can, which he had been organizing, posting and exhibiting since 2022 (Chapters 13 and 14). [32,3] What the public record does not say is when or how the collection began, which pieces are oldest, or who in the family started it. The only public figures are the family’s own: about 100 Black Santa figures and images and 100 Black Santa ornaments. [33] The Cape Gazette’s Dec. 8, 2025, tour story and the Dec. 7 Facebook post are the only public accounts of the collection found for this book. Earlier searches of Delaware newspapers, TV, Penn State outlets and the heritage commission found nothing more.

Penn State memorabilia. In 2020 Onward State featured his 1949 Wally Triplett collection, an autographed leather Penn State helmet, an autographed photo and Triplett’s NFL rookie card, in a story on readers’ best vintage Penn State memorabilia . [65] The archive behind the Chronicles. His research files became the documents, photos and interviews on blackhistory.psu.edu . [24]

In its September/October 2024 issue, The Penn Stater gave its editor’s column, by Ryan Jones ’95, to Darryl under the headline “A History Worth Documenting.” Its summary reads: “Darryl Daisey’s passion and dedication illuminate the stories of Black Penn Staters.” [1]

The same could be said of his work in Lewes. The public record traced in this book follows one thread from start to finish. A Lewes family had to send a son 90 miles away to finish high school, and that son became a city councilman and a tribal chief. His wife led a Black Girl Scout troop when the town’s troop would not admit Black girls, and their oldest children helped integrate the town’s schools. One of those children, a business logistics graduate who spent his career in supply chains, became the person Penn State and Lewes turn to when they want to know their Black history. He compiled it, published it, gave it away, lent his family’s photographs to museums, and in 2026 chaired the city commission charged with preserving it. [5,9,70]

In his own words, history “tells you why you’re here.” [48] His sons, his nephews and the young Girl Scouts who left Bethel church with patches reading “A Journey to the Past” are part of the reason he keeps documenting it. [37] “Penn State would not be Penn State without its people of color.”Darryl Daisey, April 2, 2025, as headlined by The Daily Collegian [48]
